strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and increasingly important problem: the growing IO/memory bottleneck in fine-grained, sparse MoE training as models trend toward higher granularity and sparsity (well supported by Table 1's survey of real frontier models).

Technically deep and novel kernel-level contributions: memory-efficient backward algorithm (avoiding caching Y, dY, dO_e) that provably matches the activation memory of a dense model with equivalent activated parameters, plus detailed Hopper/Blackwell-specific overlap strategies (Ping-Pong scheduling, TMA vs cp.async gather/scatter tradeoffs, tensor memory usage on Blackwell).

Extensive and carefully controlled empirical evaluation: comparisons against many strong baselines (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM/DeepGEMM++) across model scales from 1.4B to 685B, with both synthetic and real open-source model configurations (Figure 15), and detailed component-level ablations (Appendix E) isolating the effect of gather fusion, epilogue fusion, scatter vs TMA store, and top-K kernel design.

Novel token rounding (TR) routing algorithm is theoretically clean (bounded to a single tile deviation from top-K) and empirically validated for quality preservation across multiple model scales and sparsity regimes (0.5B-1.8B), with thorough ablations on rounding subroutine, microbatch size, and tile size sensitivity.

Demonstrates real end-to-end training throughput gains (213B vs 225B tokens/day using appreciably fewer GPUs, 64 vs 96 H100s) rather than only synthetic kernel microbenchmarks, improving practical credibility.
Open-sourced kernels and codebase, and very detailed appendices (notation tables, algorithmic pseudocode, benchmark configs) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Token rounding's quality preservation is only validated at relatively small scales (up to 1.8B parameters, ≤100B tokens), while the throughput benchmarks are shown at much larger configurations (7B-685B); it remains unclear whether TR's quality-preservation guarantees extend to production-scale training runs matching the kernel throughput experiments.

The headline end-to-end comparison (213B tokens/day on 64 H100s for SonicMoE vs 225B tokens/day on 96 H100s for ScatterMoE) uses different GPU counts, and while the authors frame this favorably, a matched-hardware comparison would make the throughput claim more directly interpretable.

The paper is systems/kernel-engineering heavy with substantial low-level GPU architecture detail (CUTLASS, TMA, warpgroups, tensor memory); this may be less accessible or evaluable by a general AI audience and could be a better fit for a systems-focused venue, even though the topic is highly relevant to efficient LLM training.

Token rounding is fundamentally a training-time approximation (not usable directly at inference without switching back to TC), and the paper does not deeply explore robustness of this train/inference mismatch beyond the small-scale experiments, nor its interaction with expert-parallel deployment settings.

Given the complexity of the described kernel engineering, exact reproducibility for non-specialist readers may be challenging despite code release, and some comparisons (e.g., DeepGEMM++ being an in-house extension of DeepGEMM) may not be independently verifiable baselines.

Limited discussion of how the approach interacts with expert-parallel communication overlap (mentioned only as future work), which is important for very large-scale training where all-to-all costs often dominate.

strengths: Extensive and detailed systems engineering effort spanning memory-efficient forward/backward algorithm design, IO-aware kernel fusion, and a novel tile-aware token-rounding routing method.

Broad empirical coverage across model scales (1.4B to 685B-parameter configurations) and against many baselines (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM/DeepGEMM++), with detailed kernel-level profiling breakdowns.
The activation-memory reduction claim (constant w.r.t. granularity, up to 45% savings) is well justified analytically and empirically validated across scales.

Token rounding is evaluated not just for throughput but also for downstream task quality preservation across several sparsity/granularity settings, with reasonably thorough ablations on rounding subroutines, microbatch size, and tile size.
Open-sourcing of kernels and detailed appendix documentation (notation, algorithms, comparison tables) aids reproducibility and understanding of design choices.
weaknesses: The single genuine end-to-end training throughput comparison (213B vs 225B tokens/day) shows SonicMoE on 64 H100s only matching, not exceeding, ScatterMoE on 96 H100s — a comparatively underwhelming real-world validation relative to the large synthetic-kernel speedups (e.g., 1.86x, 50%) emphasized in the abstract/intro, raising concerns about how well microbenchmark gains translate to full training pipelines.

All large-scale (30B-685B) results are single-GPU/single-layer microbenchmarks without expert parallelism; since real large sparse MoE training relies heavily on expert-parallel communication (all2all, EP), the lack of any expert-parallel or multi-node evaluation limits confidence that the reported gains hold in realistic large-scale training regimes.

The core novelty is primarily systems/kernel engineering (fusion, Ping-Pong scheduling adapted from FlashAttention-3, gather/scatter optimization) rather than new algorithmic or modeling insight; token rounding is also conceptually close to prior capacity-factor/token-dropping and rectify-router ideas.

Token rounding requires switching back to token-choice routing at inference/eval time (train-test mismatch), an architectural compromise similar to the EC-routing limitations the paper itself criticizes, yet this mismatch and its risks are not deeply analyzed at larger scale or over longer training runs.

Quality-preservation experiments for token rounding are conducted only at small scale (0.5B–1.8B parameters, 20–100B tokens); it remains unclear whether these findings generalize to frontier-scale MoE training with trillions of tokens where routing dynamics may differ substantially.

The paper's extreme density of hardware-specific implementation detail (CUTLASS/CuTe-DSL, Blackwell TMEM specifics, warp-level scheduling) makes it very difficult for reviewers to independently verify many of the finer technical/numerical claims without direct access to and exercise of the released code.

Reported speedups are drawn from a large number of specific configurations without variance/repetition statistics, and comparisons to baselines that reportedly 'fail to run' or are otherwise handicapped (e.g., DeepGEMM lacking certain kernels, so a custom 'DeepGEMM++' is constructed) raise some concern about the fairness/representativeness of chosen comparison points.

strengths: Comprehensive systems contribution: the paper co-designs MoE algorithm and GPU kernels across three complementary axes (activation-memory-efficient backward algorithm, IO-aware Hopper/Blackwell kernel design with gather fusion and Ping-Pong scheduling, and tile-aware token rounding routing), each addressing a distinct and well-motivated inefficiency in modern fine-grained/sparse MoE training.

Strong empirical grounding: extensive kernel-level benchmarking across model scales (1.4B to 685B), with detailed ablations isolating the effect of each design choice (gather fusion on M vs K dims, epilogue fusion, Ping-Pong scheduling, top-K kernel design) against multiple strong baselines (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM).

Clear and substantial quantitative gains: 45% activation memory reduction, up to 1.86x compute throughput improvement, and demonstrated end-to-end training throughput on real FSDP-2 training runs (213B tokens/day on 64 H100s vs 225B on 96 H100s for ScatterMoE), showing practical, not just synthetic, benefits.

The token rounding routing idea is a simple, elegant, and hardware-motivated technique that is validated not only for throughput but also for downstream task quality preservation across multiple model scales (0.5B-1.8B) and sparsity regimes, with thorough ablations on rounding subroutines, microbatch size, and tile size.

Good scholarly honesty and rigor: detailed technical comparison table (Table 2) and appendix section explicitly enumerating differences from prior kernels, careful discussion of architectural constraints (e.g., Blackwell 2-CTA relay mechanism), and transparent discussion of what SonicMoE does not solve (e.g., atomic-add determinism issues).
Commitment to open-sourcing kernels, which enhances reproducibility and potential community impact given the practical relevance to widely used MoE architectures.
weaknesses: The paper focuses entirely on single-GPU/single-node kernel throughput and memory; there is no evaluation of expert-parallel or distributed training settings (all2all overlap, communication-computation overlap for EP) despite this being explicitly flagged as important future work, limiting the demonstrated relevance to the largest-scale MoE models mentioned in the motivation (e.g., Kimi K2, DeepSeek V3.2).

Downstream task evaluations for token rounding are conducted only on small-scale (0.5B-1.8B parameter) models trained on relatively few tokens (20-100B), which may not fully predict behavior at the frontier scales (100B+ params, trillions of tokens) that motivate the paper's granularity/sparsity trends in Table 1.

The real end-to-end training throughput comparison (213B vs 225B tokens/day on 64 vs 96 H100s) is presented as a headline result but is a single data point without variance, and the different GPU counts across the two systems make direct comparison somewhat approximate; more configurations or a matched-hardware comparison would strengthen this claim.

Some quality metrics for token rounding show mixed results (e.g., in Table 3 EC or TC-drop baselines occasionally outperform TR on subsets of downstream tasks), and the claim of 'no accuracy loss' could be moderated given this variance, especially since only one softmax renormalization scheme and one tile size default are used as primary configuration.

The paper is very dense and kernel-engineering-heavy with limited high-level intuition/theory beyond arithmetic-intensity analysis; broader ML audience may find it hard to assess correctness of low-level claims (e.g., CUDA/TMA pipeline details) without independent verification, relying heavily on the released code for reproducibility.

strengths: Comprehensive systems contribution spanning three complementary techniques: a memory-efficient MoE backward algorithm, IO-aware kernel design (gather/epilogue fusion, Ping-Pong scheduling on Hopper and TMEM-based overlap on Blackwell), and a novel tile-aware token rounding routing method — each independently useful and well-motivated by a clear arithmetic-intensity analysis.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of model scales (1.4B to 685B-parameter configurations matching real open-source MoE architectures like DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-Next, Kimi-Linear, gpt-oss), and across two GPU generations (H100 and B300), with detailed kernel-level runtime breakdowns.
Strong, credible real end-to-end training throughput validation using FSDP-2 on 64-96 H100s (213B vs 225B tokens/day) rather than only synthetic microbenchmarks, which substantiates practical impact.

Very thorough ablation studies (appendices F and G) isolating the contribution of gather fusion, epilogue fusion, aggregation strategy, top-K kernel design, and different token-rounding subroutines, and studying sensitivity to microbatch size and tile size.

Token rounding is validated not just for speed but for downstream task quality across multiple model sizes/sparsity regimes (Table 2), with a solid comparison against reasonable alternative baselines (EC with auxiliary router, EC with TC finetuning, token dropping).

Clear, detailed comparison table (Table 1) and appendix discussion (Appendix B) contrasting SonicMoE's design choices against ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, and DeepGEMM, showing careful positioning relative to prior work.
Code and kernels are open-sourced with a permissive license, aiding reproducibility and practical adoption by the community.

Mathematically rigorous derivation showing the proposed dS/dH computation path avoids caching Y/dY without added FLOPs, and clear proof-like guarantees for token rounding's bounded deviation from top-K routing.
weaknesses: The core techniques (gather/epilogue fusion, Ping-Pong overlap of MMA and IO, tile-based token rounding) are largely engineering optimizations and hardware-specific applications of known GEMM-optimization concepts (e.g., from FlashAttention-3) rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas, which may limit the paper's broader intellectual novelty despite its practical value.

Token rounding's quality preservation is only validated on relatively small models (0.5B-1.8B parameters) trained on modest token budgets (20-100B tokens), leaving open whether the reported quality parity holds at the scale of the very large sparse models (100B-1T+ params, trillions of tokens) that motivate the paper's introduction.

Some baselines used for comparison (e.g., "DeepGEMM++") are custom, author-constructed combinations of DeepGEMM with additional hand-written kernels, which, while reasonably justified, are not independently validated as a de facto SOTA baseline and could bias reported speedups favorably.

The paper's writing and presentation is extremely dense, with a very large number of figures/tables and terse notation, which may hinder accessibility and careful independent verification of specific claims despite the extensive appendix.

The token-rounding speedup benefits are concentrated in high-sparsity regimes; for more moderate sparsity settings common in many current models, the gains are comparatively small (e.g., ~2-8% in several configurations in Figure 14), somewhat tempering the practical significance of this specific contribution.

Discussion of low-precision (FP8/MXFP8/MXFP4) training, which is increasingly standard for frontier MoE training, is deferred entirely to future work, leaving a gap regarding the applicability of these optimizations under the precision regimes actually used by the very large models referenced (e.g., DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2).

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: training inefficiency of fine-grained, sparse MoE models on modern GPUs.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning model scales from 1.4B to 685B-equivalent configurations, on both Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B300) GPUs, with comparisons against a wide set of strong baselines (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM, Triton reference kernels).

Several concrete, well-justified technical contributions: an activation-memory-efficient backward formulation that avoids materializing Y/dO and derives dS/dH without caching large intermediate tensors, fused gather/epilogue kernels, and Ping-Pong/TMEM-based MMA-IO overlap tailored to Hopper and Blackwell architectures.

The token rounding (TR) routing algorithm is a simple, well-motivated idea (bounding deviation from top-K to at most one tile) with a reasonably rigorous theoretical guarantee and solid ablations over rounding subroutines, microbatch size, and tile size.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each design choice (gather fusion, epilogue fusion, aggregation strategy, top-K kernel) with kernel-level profiling.
Reports both micro-benchmark (TFLOPS/memory) and more realistic end-to-end training throughput numbers (tokens/day with FSDP-2), increasing credibility of claims.
Promises open-source release of kernels, which would benefit reproducibility and practical adoption.
weaknesses: The core contribution is primarily low-level systems/kernel engineering (fusion, scheduling, memory layout) rather than a new algorithmic or modeling idea; novelty relative to prior work (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, DeepGEMM, FlashAttention-3 Ping-Pong scheduling) is incremental, mostly combining and extending known techniques to the MoE setting.

Downstream quality validation of token rounding is limited to relatively small models (up to 1.8B parameters, tens of billions of training tokens), which is far from the scale (100B+ parameter, trillions of tokens) at which the sparsity/granularity trends motivating the paper actually manifest; it is unclear whether TR's quality preservation holds at frontier scale.

Several throughput comparisons rely on 'DeepGEMM++', an in-house, author-optimized variant of DeepGEMM rather than an official baseline, and on author-reimplemented Triton/Tilelang kernels; while transparently disclosed, this raises some concern about comparison fairness and reproducibility of the exact speedup numbers.

The paper explicitly defers two important practical aspects—low-precision/microscaling formats (FP8/MXFP4) and communication-computation overlap for expert-parallel distributed training—to future work, even though these are highly relevant for the large-scale, sparse, distributed MoE regimes the paper motivates itself with (e.g., Kimi K2, DeepSeek-V3.2).

Token rounding is not itself a deployable routing method for autoregressive inference (acknowledged by the authors) and the paper only evaluates a 'train with TR, switch to TC at eval' protocol without a principled inference-time adaptation, limiting the practical significance of this contribution compared to EC-routing follow-up work it critiques.

The manuscript is extremely dense with low-level implementation detail (8 kernels, warp-level scheduling, TMEM mechanics) that may hinder accessibility and broader impact assessment for a general AI audience, and the many partial/relative speedup numbers across configurations make it hard to extract a single clear headline result.

Gains are hardware- and generation-specific (Hopper/Blackwell, CUTLASS/CuTe-DSL), tying the contribution closely to current NVIDIA architectures and raising questions about longevity/generality as hardware evolves.

Task-level results for TR versus TC top-K are mixed/marginal in several settings (Table 2), so the claim of 'maintaining similar downstream performance' is only loosely supported rather than a clean win across the board.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous systems contribution: the paper tackles three distinct but complementary problems (activation memory, IO-bound kernel throughput, and tile quantization waste) with a coherent co-design philosophy spanning algorithm, kernel, and routing levels.

Strong theoretical grounding: the arithmetic intensity analysis (Eq. 4) clearly motivates why fine-grained/sparse MoEs become memory-bound, and the derivation of dS and dH without materializing Y/dY is a non-trivial and elegant mathematical reformulation that is proven to preserve correctness while cutting memory and IO.

Extensive empirical validation across two GPU generations (Hopper and Blackwell), multiple model scales (1.4B to 685B configurations), and against many strong/relevant baselines (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM, Triton reference kernels), including real end-to-end FSDP-2 training throughput numbers on 64-96 H100s, which is a meaningful and rarely-shown practical validation.

The token rounding (TR) routing method is a clever, simple, and practically useful contribution with bounded deviation guarantees (at most one tile per expert) and is validated both for training throughput gains (up to 25.7%/15.9% in sparse regimes) and for downstream task quality preservation across multiple model scales and ablations (rounding subroutine, tile size, microbatch size).

Very thorough ablation and comparison appendix (30+ pages) covering kernel-level breakdowns (gather fusion, epilogue fusion, top-K kernel, expert aggregation kernel) that isolate the contribution of each design choice, which strengthens reproducibility and credibility of the throughput claims.

The work addresses a timely and practically significant problem given the clear industry trend toward finer-grained and sparser MoEs (well documented in Table 4), and the open-sourcing of kernels adds value to the community.

Honest discussion of limitations/tradeoffs, e.g., the transient Y materialization caveat, the EC-routing inference mismatch issues, and the Blackwell 2-CTA cp.async architectural workaround, which indicates technical maturity and care.
weaknesses: The token rounding (TR) quality evaluation is done only at small scales (0.5B-1.8B parameters, 20-100B tokens) and switched to TC routing only at evaluation time rather than testing it in a setting matching real large-scale, long-horizon training runs where router training dynamics could behave differently; it's unclear how well these conclusions generalize to frontier-scale models (e.g., 70B+ with trillions of tokens).

The paper's throughput claims rely heavily on comparisons against baselines (ScatterMoE, MoMoE) that are implemented in Triton and may not represent fully optimized CUTLASS/CuTe-DSL competitors for every configuration; DeepGEMM++ is a stronger baseline but is itself an augmented/optimized version built by the authors on top of DeepGEMM, raising minor concerns about a fully independent, apples-to-apples baseline for all metrics.

Some reported end-to-end comparisons (e.g., 213B tokens/day on 64 H100s vs. 225B tokens/day on 96 H100s for ScatterMoE) mix different hardware counts, which, while informative, makes the comparison less direct than a controlled same-hardware comparison; additional discussion of cost-normalized throughput would strengthen the claim.

The paper is extremely dense with many kernel-level and architecture-specific details (CUTLASS/CuTe-DSL internals, TMEM, Ping-Pong scheduling, relay warps for Blackwell 2-CTA clusters), which, while valuable for systems experts, may limit accessibility and makes it hard to verify correctness without the released code; reproducibility hinges heavily on the promised but not-yet-visible open-source release (GitHub link appears blank/placeholder in the submission).

Token rounding's compatibility with autoregressive inference/online serving is not addressed in depth (the paper explicitly sidesteps this by switching to TC at eval time), leaving an important practical question about deployment unresolved.

The novelty of individual techniques (Ping-Pong scheduling, TMA, gather fusion) is incremental relative to known GPU programming patterns (e.g., FlashAttention-3), and the core novelty is more in the careful application/combination to the MoE setting rather than fundamentally new hardware techniques, which is acknowledged by the authors but somewhat limits the conceptual novelty score.
